utterances.text: The next matter, Your Honour, is that you had requested to see the original and inspect S84, which I have here. I don't know whether you wish to do that now or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the usher could be so kind and present it first to the Defence and then to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, we are discussing both sides of these documents? Apparently, there are two documents on two sides of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, that is the original of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So for clarification, admitted into evidence, both sides of the same document. Are there any comments on these special documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have two comments. On both occasions, Mr. Cayley mischaracterised it as being the original. For purposes of clarity in our record, these are not originals. I know we have struggled from time to time to identify documents that are considered either copies or originals from copies. I just object to that characterisation because I think in the signature block on one side, the signature is absolutely not there. And the signature on the other side, it seems to be a copy of the original print, although I'm not a forensic handwriting comparative analysis expert. I think that may have been discussed by Mr. ten Camp in his previous testimony. I object to the mischaracterisation by Mr. Cayley in connection with these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we agree that we have a document before us where we can read -- where we can see on both sides a blue stamp, and that we can read on this being a copy, we saw it the best possible original, even if it may be a copy only, and that on the top of the page, we can read written by ink some notes on this document. Can we agree on this basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Although our comments since the Court invited us with respect to limited -- with respect to this document is that we would like to find the sourcing of it, number one, which I think we've already established; but number two, some information as to how is it possible that there would be a copied signature followed by an original stamp. And I'm only stating that for the record so that it's clear when we are discussing this S84 that it's clear on this document, at the very least from my observation, there's a copy, a signature that seems to be copied but yet with an original stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Point also on documents issued by this Tribunal, copy but then added with an original stamp. I think there's nothing special with this. But for the list of exhibits, it should be included that both sides of this are admitted. And I'm afraid, we have only one side copied until now. And I would appreciate if we could get, once again, colour copies from both sides of this document. From both sides? It's already from... Yes, I can see it from here. Okay. Thank you. Just for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next matter, Mr. President, is the document that you requested, which is the 8316 Prijedor Territorial Defence document. And if I can offer that. Do you wish me to put this in front of the witness just to confirm this is the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would just add, Mr. President, at the moment that is a draft translation, and we are seeking an authorised translation. But for the immediate benefit of the Court, we had that done. But we are getting an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it be presented to the Defence, and then to the Judges as well. S361. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: S362, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 362. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then next, Your Honour, you wished to see, and I'll be careful about using this word original, the order of the 6th Krajina Brigade is a photographic copy. It is the best original that we have. As I think I explained yesterday, this is a document that was photocopied, and the original returned to the Bosnian government. So if I can show that to the Defence and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to address the Court, if I may, on this document, although I'm not sure whether the Court would rather that you have the document before you before I make my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be excellent if we would know what it's about. Please, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Cayley indicates in his remarks in connection with this document that the original was purportedly returned to the Bosnian government. As the Court can plainly see on the first page of the document where it discusses the 6th Partizan Brigade, if I recall correctly, the number 6 is handwritten in there, and my question is whether or not the original document had the 6 on it handwritten in there or if in the interim a handwritten number 6 was placed on it. And I think for purposes of the record, when Mr. Cayley identifies a document that he simply doesn't identify the document in the manner that would suggest it's all typewritten script. These documents from the Defence's perspective are being called into question because of the additional handwriting materials provided on the document. And we also have, we think, on the second page issues with respect to the authenticity of the signature as well as the stamp, if I recall correctly, appearing on the page. So those would be our objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document was already admitted into evidence. We appreciate your comments and take it into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then lastly, Your Honour, you will recall that the witness -- I think you asked the witness a number of questions about this document because there were concerns about its authenticity. And he stated to you that he had corroborated it through other original sources, and he referred to a footnote in that respect. And I haven't got both of them; I have just simply got one of them which he used to corroborate that document. And if I could show that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just simply, Mr. Brown, is that one of the documents that you were referring to that you had used to corroborate the 6th Partizan Brigade document in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honours. It's one of the documents that indicates operations in the Carakovo and other areas. And it's from the 1st Krajina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it the intention to tender this as it appears only now as Footnote 142.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender it as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please correct me, would it be S362? S363, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think that concludes the administrative matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe I have overlooked something. I'm still fighting with a deluge of documents provided because we are grateful to have the basis for your expertise. But I recall that there was a document presented yesterday on these VP numbers where in handwriting it was added this 8316.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is the document, Your Honour, that I just presented to you a moment ago which actually has the handwritten TO 8316. S362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. But please recall that there were some doubts and, to the best of the my recollection, the witness said "I believe this is it" or whatever he said. And we needed some clarification on this. And may I ask Mr. Brown directly, could you come closer to that what brought you to the conclusion that there is this link between 8316 and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document which has just been tendered in relation to the equipment supply indicates that one TAM truck with -- was to be provided to TO 8316 Prijedor. And I believe 8316 Prijedor is indicated on the distribution list of that document. I think that's the document dated some time in February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document S362, there it reads in paragraph 3 under 2: "Prijedor TO, 8316 will take over the mobile workshop fixed on a track..." and so on. And this is the basis for your conclusion, that 8316 is the Prijedor TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask, Judge Fassi Fihri, do you have any additional questions? Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I would like you to help us to properly understand the development and the outcome of engagement in the area of Kozarac village between 25th and 27th of May, 1992. According to the report of the 1st Krajina Corps command of May 27th, 1992, the participants of this -- it's in Exhibit Number S350, ERN number 00938549. According to this report, the participants of this engagement were, on the one hand, the 343 Motorised Brigade, an enlarged motorised battalion supported by two Horitzer batteries and one tank squadron. On the other hand, the Green Beret, numbering 15 to 20.000 men without heavy weapons. What was numerical strength of the Serb forces? Can you tell us, approximately.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't specifically state what the exact numeric strength of either a reinforced motorised battalion from the brigade was. The 343rd Motorised Brigade by late May consisted, I believe, of nearly 5.000 men, and that comes from figures in military documentation of the Corps. A motorized battalion can vary, and I wouldn't want to quote figures from the battalion where the documentations don't make it clear. There were a number of battalions within the brigade, so it's a subordination of the brigade. The two 105-millimetre howitzer batteries I would assess consisted of around 12 individual 105 millimetre howitzer guns. It was in the JNA that there were about six individual guns within a battery. I can't tell you the number of personnel that would be manning those two batteries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable I think to give you specific numbers. I would imagine that the motorised battalion would run into hundreds of soldiers. It could be anything up to a thousand soldiers, a battalion. The 5th Brigade -- sorry the 343rd Brigade was a very large brigade indeed, in comparison to many other brigades of the core. The M-84 tank platoon normally consists of about four tanks, four individual tanks, and with their composite crews of about four or five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And then which participating side was attacking, and which one was in the defence?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 343rd Brigade was attacking the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Now, according to the military theory and practice of armed conflicts, what is normal average, approximate ratio, of casualties in land warfare engagements when one adversary is attacking another who is in defensive position?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very difficult question for me to answer with a lot of specificity. However, attacking in a semi-urban area often is not the preferred terrain for a military to attack because the advantage is normally with the defender. Semi-urban or urban areas can very easily be defended by military units. It can be very time consuming to clear semi-urban or urban environments. And from my own experience in the military, it is one of the most time consuming, demanding, logistically draining operations the military can involve itself in. The advantage is always with the defender, and from my own training, the attacker normally suffers significant casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And why in this -- the report states that -- the document, the Exhibit Number S350, that Serbian casualties were five killed and 20 wounded, and the Green Beret casualties were 100 - 200 persons, 80 - 100 Green Berets were killed. How to explain it? So army of Republika Srpska invented new radical methods of warfare or used?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe for that type of terrain that the casualty figures for the Serb military were particularly high. I can only assess that the defence was not particularly robust or effective, and that an area which is semi-urbanised was -- the control of that area was taken over very quickly, adding to my assessment that the defence was very weak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following on the customs in this courtroom, we just before conferred. It's now for the defence to discuss, or to put additional questions emanating from the Judges' questions, but also from those put forward by the OTP. And no doubt, if necessary, it's then for the OTP. I think in this environment, and especially with our mandate to come as close as possible to the truth, we should discuss the issues until both parties are satisfied. Please, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, help me with this: From a military standpoint when you state on page 51, lines 18 through 19, when the Honourable Court asked you the question, you answered in part that it would be "very time consuming to clear semi-urban and urban environment." When you say "clear," sir, doesn't that mean militarily speaking, and only militarily speaking, mopping up?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I used the word "clear," I mean from my own perspective when I was serving in the military, would be to take control of the territory and kill or destroy the enemy that were defending it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention, with the assistance of the usher, to Exhibit 71 which we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour, while madam usher is presenting that exhibit just so I get my question and Mr. Brown can digest it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, tell me if you know, if a hospital in a municipality, where there are injured, wounded citizens from the municipality, and if someone were to call to have security placed in that hospital so that those that are being treated for their wounds can be adequately provided the security, is that a link under your definition for responsibility? And as you see specifically Exhibit S71 discusses providing security for a hospital, does it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there anything wrong with individuals, including political individuals, calling the police and asking them to provide security to a public institution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that bad?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness is not here to say whether or not an order is good or bad. We are looking at this in respect of whether or not it's an order, whether this has a directive instruction within it. It has nothing to do with the goodness or badness of what is being requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to Exhibit S72. And because -- let me make sure I have this right, because I would hate to misquote things here. You being a "normal, objective, conservative person," can you read S72 and as you say in your response to that question of your style, Mr. Brown, that from the face of it you can make an assessment. From the face of S72, in your normal, objective, and conservative style, can you tell me whether or not that is with regard to the search of Muslim citizens, Serb citizens, Croat citizens, or other citizens within the Prijedor Municipality, or does it, based upon a normal, objective conservative style, on its face, it really discusses all the citizens of Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness has answered this question already several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to S79, if I may. As a provision while the madam usher is providing you a copy of that. I'm sure you can recall the document. You rely on it. You have just reviewed it when Mr. Cayley was asking you questions. It's one of basic tasks, I think, one of the words that's presented in that document. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The phrase "basic task" is contained within this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anywhere within that document when it was ordered to take care of a basic task which is specifically set forth there such as preventing looting or other criminal activities, does it suggest anywhere within that document, sir, that that is a request to prevent Muslims from looting or Muslims from performing criminal activities, or does it, sir, actually reflect that the civil authorities wanted to preserve some order of a semblance of peace, an order that there should be a prevention of looting and other criminal activities as it relates to all the citizens of Prijedor? And tell me if you can, keeping it in your normal, objective, conservative style.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order at face value, as it's written, makes no distinction but is an order to the police and to the regional command to form a joint intervention platoon with the basic task of preventing looting and other criminal activities in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no further questions. This concludes your testimony. Thank you for -- I have to thank you for preparing the report and patiently answering all the questions from both sides. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You're excused. And may I ask madam usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me take the opportunity as regards the remaining one and a half day scheduling. There are two options: Either we do the necessary technical work, that is, first of all, admission into evidence of some additional documents and all the remaining points on the agenda today in the presence of the three Judges, save the parties would agree that this can be done tomorrow in the presence of two Judges only and, furthermore, if necessary, even tomorrow in the afternoon if it should be necessary to extend the hearing until afternoon, which I don't hope it will be necessary. So would you, (a), consent to do this in the presence of two Judges; and (b), if necessary, to extend the 15 bis rule on tomorrow afternoon as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We will consent. We have no objection to that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Defence consents to the manner of proceeding as the Court suggests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Then we can proceed with the next witness. And this will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Corin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No protective --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Corin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No protective measures? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, you'll excuse me now from the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, we distributed today a spreadsheet -- it's our intention. It actually is an updated and corrected version of a document we distributed earlier which I indicate I had some reservations about. It has since been rechecked and a few corrections made and put into an order, I think, which is much more user friendly in that all the documents are ordered by the S number. I believe that was S291. Is that right? 296. May this spreadsheet be substituted for S296, the previous version? This is the more accurate and updated version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think, for clarity, it is better to have it as S296-1, what we are discussing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, we do not vouch for the accuracy of the earlier version, and I think I indicated at the time that I had some reservations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Only that we know what we are discussing, the former or the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Corin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before starting, may we please hear your solemn declaration. Would you please stand up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. And Mr. Koumjian, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Channel 4 is English, Doctor. Dr. Corin, would you please tell the Court what is your current employment.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I am currently employed by the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY as a research officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How long have you worked for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I have worked for the Office of the Prosecutor continuously since February of the year 2001. Prior to that time, I worked on a temporary basis between June of 1999 and December of the same year, and again between June of the year 2000 and February of the year 2001. At that earlier period, I was employed here temporarily as I was on leave from my position at the University of California at Los Angeles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to briefly go through your educational background. Can you tell us if you have an undergraduate degree and from where you obtained that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I have the diploma, which is approximately equivalent to a bachelor's degree, from the faculty of philology at the University of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In addition to this degree, did you do any graduate studies? And if so, tell us where and when you obtained a diploma.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I pursued graduate study at the University of California, Los Angeles in the department of Slavic languages and literatures. I received the degree of master of arts in the year 1979. I continued on and received the degree of doctor of philosophy in the year 1986 in the same department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What languages do you speak?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: My native language is English. I regularly speak in my home life in what we used to call Serbo-Croatian and what we in this institution refer to Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian. I speak Russian. And with ever-decreasing fluency can occasionally make myself understood in a number of other languages including French, German, a variety of Slavic languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Since you mentioned your home life, can you tell us where your spouse is from.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: My spouse is from the Former Yugoslavia, precisely from the Vojvodina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Corin, were you given a request to prepare a report for this Court in answer from a request from the Bench from the Judges?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did you prepare that report originally dated the 5th of September, 2002, "Characteristics of a Corpus of Documents Associated with the Name of Milomir Stakic", and have you recently submitted an updated version correcting a few minor errors.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did produce the report dated 5th of September, and I did recently submit the slightly updated version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the report be admitted into evidence, given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, please correct me, S364. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe, to put the correct date on the record, it's dated the 25th of September, 2002. And I'm sorry, Your Honour, apparently it already has an exhibit number, Ms. Karper tells me, of S295. But that apparently was the earlier version, so perhaps we should keep this number for the 25th of September version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That we have a kind of system, I think the updated version should go as S259-1. What about the CV? Separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sure. May that be marked. We have copies. I believe the Court already has it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the CV would be S364, but we have exhausted this number. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Corin, in addition to preparing --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. But S295-1 was already attributed to an attachment to the report previously submitted. So therefore the report dated 25 September should be S295-3? 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Corin, in addition to preparing the report, did you assist in the preparation of a document that has now been given the exhibit number S296-1 that I'm holding in my hands, Milomir Stakic, authorship of decisions, orders, and conclusions and other documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did assist in the preparation of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in fact, was it -- did you prepare the column "original document" based upon reviewing the copies of the documents in evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me clarify when I say "in evidence," the best copy that's available to the OTP, that which the evidence unit had?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did you also supervise some other individuals on the team who were preparing or checking on this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did. On an occasional basis, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I do not want to go through all of the details of your report, but just highlight several of the major conclusions. In order to understand your task, did you actually review a transcript of His Honour Judge Schomburg's request regarding an analysis of the documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Following the review of that transcript, did you formulate the request into five separate -- I believe it's five separate questions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going to the first question indicated in your report, did you attempt to study the documents in order to determine whether they could be linked through any type of referencing within a document or to other documents in this group that you examined?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did. My result, briefly, would be that in many instances, yes, this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And how were documents linked by -- between each other? In what manner did you observe links?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: In many of these documents, we find reference numbers which presumably identify this document as opposed to all other documents. Where a document has a reference number, usually this reference number is similar to the reference numbers found in some other documents. When this is the case, the groups of documents which have similar reference numbers have these reference numbers form a sequence, usually with gaps but nevertheless what seemed to be parts of a recognisable sequence. Beyond this linking through the sequences of reference numbers, there were some instances in which we find one document of this corpus of documents that I was examining which contains references to other documents within this same corpus of documents. This is especially and primarily the case in regard to the document which, if I recall correctly, bears the 65 ter number 297.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the record, that is S250. Is that the document that you refer to in your -- did you give it a name in your report, that particular document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: In my report, I refer to this document as the "confirmation document." Now, perhaps I should point out at this moment, I realise that in the accompanying annex, I see that it is referred to as a confirming rather than confirmation document. The reference is to the same item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the sequence of numbers. Was there anything in the documents that you examined that could lead you to conclude that there perhaps were orders or conclusions that you did not or that the OTP did not have?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes. There were considerable gaps in the sequences of reference numbers on the documents in the corpus that I was analysing. It quickly became clear to me that many documents, or perhaps many acts, bearing intervening reference numbers could be seen -- could be found published in the Official Gazette of the Prijedor Municipality. It also became clear that some acts which appear to be identical or very, very similar to those represented in the corpus are also published in the Official Gazette, with usually the same reference number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that even in the Official Gazette, there appears to be some gaps in the numbering indicating that, for whatever reason, some documents were not published?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the confirmation document. Can you just give a very quick description of that document.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: This is a document of, as I recall, I believe 14 pages, 13 or 14 pages. It consists of I would say three major parts. The first is an introduction stating that this, what will follow, is a list of acts of the Crisis Staff and war presidency of the municipality of Prijedor which are being or which will be submitted for confirmation or verification to the Municipal Assembly of the Prijedor Municipality. This is followed by the list in question. And at the end of this document, we find what appears to be a proposed Municipal Assembly decision confirming or verifying the acts on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In addition to the documents being linked to each other by reference numbers or to the confirmation document, did you see other indications that documents that, for example, appeared to be signed, that there was other evidence that these, in fact, were documents that had been officially adopted?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: There were, if I recall correctly, two at least documents of the Crisis Staff to which reference is made in the newspaper Kozarski Vjesnik. Furthermore, a number of Municipal Assembly acts, which appear to be present in our corpus of documents in draft form, are referred to in the newspaper Kozarski Vjesnik in reference to a Municipal Assembly session which, as I recall, took place on 27 August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned documents that appear to you to be in draft form. Is that because some of them did not have a complete number or signature or stamp?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On any of these documents, did you observe any evidence from your review of the Official Gazette that these decisions had been adopted indeed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did, indeed. I've provided in the report a list of those draft documents which appear later to have been adopted by the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. In some cases, they appear to have been adopted in exactly the form in which we find them in our draft documents; in some instances, they appear to have been amended between the time that the drafts were prepared and the time when the act in question was finally adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to move on to the second question addressed in your report. Did you form an opinion as to whether there was a consistency or identity of language and terminology used in the versions of the documents that were -- that you read?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did reach such a conclusion. The language in all of these documents is what I can refer to as standard western Serbian, bearing in mind that terminology referring to this language or languages has itself been in a state of flux over the last, especially the last two decades. But I think I will be well understood if I refer to standard western Serbian as what we find in these documents with occasional intrusion into these documents of features which would be considered substandard, occasional errors which seem to reflect more the either haste or incomplete editing rather than actual linguistic characteristics of the preparer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have about a half hour of questions for the doctor. Do you want to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourn until half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Corin, you just explained your analysis of the language used in these documents. You provided us with your education. Can you also tell us since receiving your Ph.D., where have you been employed prior to coming to work for the Tribunal, for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Prior to joining the Office of the Prosecutor, I was employed for a number of years at the University of California at Los Angeles in the department of Slavic languages and literatures. Prior to that, I was employed in the department of modern languages at Pomona College.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say you were employed at those universities, or the university UCLA and Pomona College, what did you do? In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: At the University of California at Los Angeles, I was an adjunct associate professor of Slavic languages and literatures. My teaching responsibilities included the language or languages which we now call Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian here at the Tribunal. I also taught courses in Slavic linguistics, especially south Slavic linguistics, and in Slavic, and especially south Slavic cultural history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The third question addressed in your report is whether there are features common to some or all of the documents. Can you summarise your findings after reviewing the documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I've already referred to the similarity in language which is found in these documents, similarities also occurred with occasional variation in the terminology used, but overall terminology was consistent. Various documents within this corpus have similarities in regard to the signatures which occur in them, the -- many are associated with, for instance, the form of signature in Latinic script that may be read S. Milomir. There are a smaller number of documents with a signature in the Cyrillic script which may be read simply "Stakic." And I should note, on the basis of my subsequent examination of the original documents, that one document has the Cyrillic signature which is clearly "M. Stakic." It has an M. before the Stakic. I believe that this is the document bearing the -- again, I tend to recall the 65 ter numbers best. I believe it's number 69. Other than forms of signature, many of the documents share a similar form of stamp. The stamp which is primarily repeated is a stamp of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly which we find on a number of documents issued by the Crisis Staff as well as one document of the Municipal Assembly. Now, also what I have been able to ascertain beyond what is noted in the report is that these signatures wherever they are sufficiently legible contain a number. This number is found near the centre, close to the logo in the centre of the stamp. Where it is legible, this number is either a number 4, or it is a number 8, though I would add the further qualification that in some instances, the left portion of what appears to be the number 8 has not left a sufficient impression so that it can't be entirely clear that it is an 8 and not a 3. But I believe that this is in every case an 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment. Reading your answer on the screen, you indicated that what is noted in the report is that these signatures, wherever they are sufficiently legible, contain a number. Did you mean signatures?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I meant stamp, or stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you speak about things you noted subsequently or beyond the report, are you referring to after completing and submitting the report to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And after that time, did you get an opportunity to actually view the originals of the documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. And again, defining originals, the copy that is with the evidence unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I believe that this is correct. In each case, these were copies that bore coloured ERN stamps on them indicating that they were, I believe, to be the original copies that we had received into evidence, or received at ICTY with, I believe, one exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you notice any similarities in the paper that was used?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes. There are a number of different types of paper that we can find in these documents. They differ in weight. They differ in quality. I don't feel qualified to reach conclusions on the specific number of paper types. However, I did notice that several of the documents in this corpus of documents contain a watermark. For those who don't understand what a watermark is, this is a pattern impressed into paper at the time of its production. Usually you have to hold the paper up to a light source in order to read the watermark. The watermark that I found on, I believe, three documents of this corpus of documents is similar to one that I have previously in my experience as a research officer seen on, I believe, at least two other documents from the Prijedor Municipality that are not associated with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You talked about the script of the signatures, being some Latin and some Cyrillic. Are you familiar with Cyrillic handwriting, and can you tell the Court, what is your familiarity with handwriting in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I am familiar with Cyrillic handwriting, having lived in the Former Yugoslavia from early 1971 until late 1976 in an area in which Cyrillic was widely used. I encountered Cyrillic on a regular basis, I can safely say a daily basis. And it's probably safe to say that I encountered Cyrillic handwritten script almost that often. I have some professional experience dealing with Cyrillic script, much of this experience deals with the medieval period, and is part of my training and research in the field of medieval text analysis of Cyrillic documents. But occasionally, I have had to read Cyrillic handwriting in the course of my professional life as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In your report you also discuss some of the typefaces used in the documents, and some being in Cyrillic. Did you have any practical experience with typefaces from your student days in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: From my student days -- well, my greatest experience with typefaces actually came from a period of my graduate student training when for a period of I believe it was two years I was a typesetter for a professional journal. Previously, in the Former Yugoslavia, I occasionally would use a typewriter. I did not own a typewriter, but had occasion to use one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the documents, did you note any notations regarding distribution, and was there any similarities among the documents in that respect?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes. Documents of the Crisis Staff often contain both handwritten and typed annotations in regard to distribution. The typed I should rather say instructions -- I think it's not correct to refer to them as annotations -- are usually found in the lower left-hand corner of documents and indicate to whom the document in question should be -- who should receive copies of the document in question. In handwriting, at the upper right-hand corner of a number of these documents, we can see a handwritten annotations with a word which appears to be Raspis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you spell, that please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. The word is spelled R-a-s-p-i-s. It often looks as though it were spelled R-o-s-p-i-s, but I'm aware of no such word. The word spelled R-a-s-p-i-s is a bureaucratic term which is used to indicate reproduction of multiple copies of an official document for distribution. In these documents where we see this annotation, this is followed by in most cases numbers 1, or 1 and 2, or 1 and 2 and 3 and names, which I take to be names of people who are intended to receive copies of these documents. I think in one or two at least of these documents, we have also a number, for instance, a number in one document a number 13 followed by an X, and surrounded by a circle which I infer to mean 13 times or 13 copies. Also, some of these documents will, near the handwritten annotation to which I've just referred, will contain checkmarks. At the bottom of several documents, we see a handwritten word which I'll pronounce the B/C/S, and then I will spell it for you. The word Uruceno, and the spelling is U-r-u-c-e-n-o, followed by what appears to be a date. I believe the date in some or all of these documents is 9 June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And can you explain, did that have any significance to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: This indicates to me that in all likelihood, these were copies intended to be retained by the Crisis Staff, either for their archives or for some purpose known best to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I gather from your answer that the word Uruceno means archive?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I should have explained this. The word Uruceno, the word U-r-u-c-e-n-o, means delivered personally. It literally means handed, handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Moving on to the fourth issue addressed in your report, you address the issue of whether during the period from the 30th of April through the 30th of September, there was a practice among members of Crisis Staffs to sign official documents with a first or given name or with some abbreviation of the family name followed by the first or given name. Have you seen that outside of the S. Milomir signature?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I can state with confidence that I have never before or since seen a signature which recognisably consisted of the initial letter of the last name followed by the first name, certainly written together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In that, you also indicated that some signatures, Stakic in Cyrillic, and you also indicated M. Stakic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: One document has M. Stakic, the others appear to have Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was there anything noticeable about these Cyrillic script used? Was it normal Cyrillic script or did it have any remarkable characteristics?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Remarkable might be overstating the matter slightly. However, the letter K or K is formed in the manner typical of Latin script. I do not believe that this is the only time I have ever seen this occur, but nevertheless, this is the Latin form of the letter K. I believe on one occasion, the letter T or T is misformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In your experience, in that area of Bosnia, if you know, would it be common for someone to be accustomed to writing their name in either Latin or Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: In my experience - now, my experience in Western Bosnia is perhaps more limited than my experience certainly in Bosnia as a whole in reading handwritten documents and handwritten signatures, and less than my experience in reading similar documents from other areas of the country, or the Former Yugoslavia, where Cyrillic was used. But -- I'm sorry, now I've lost the train of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you believe that a person would get into a habit of writing their name in either Latin or Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: In my experience, many people are able to use one script or the other, but usually have one preferred script and usually, unless they have some reason to switch, will stick to that script.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if following the formation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Republika Srpska, there was a movement to use Cyrillic instead of Latin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I'm aware that there were a number of attempts to, as it was usually put, maintain the Cyrillic script which I take to be a -- to mean that there was an, in general, a tendency to favour the use of Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Moving on to the last question, did you form any opinions or conclusions regarding the issue of whether during the period from the 30th of April through the 30th of September, 1992, there was a consistent pattern of conduct or a particular methodology in the way documents of the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff were drafted, authorised, or signed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Since I was not present in Prijedor at this time and was not able to follow the process of document preparation, my conclusions must be based on the documents themselves; they must be inferences based on what I find within this corpus of documents. I can state that beyond those aspects of preparation which are manifest from the format of the documents themselves, there were some instances in which it appears that -- one conclusion that I made -- now, this is a conclusion based on my observations actually following a completion of this report when I've had an opportunity to look at other related documents -- I've noted that we have in our collection a number of distinct copies of documents which are -- documents of this corpus, these distinct copies are identical to the copies in the corpus other than in the fact that both have an original stamp in purple ink. Both documents will be reproductions. Both will have the original signature reproduced together with the document, but they will have a purple stamp, which would appear to be an indication that it was a common practice or at least it was a practice to produce multiple copies of documents together with a signature, and then merely apply a new stamp to each, this for purposes of distributing presumably to a fairly broad number of recipients.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the defence. You're prepared for cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are ready, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Together with Mr. Ostojic, we will continue the cross-examination in front of this Trial Chamber. My examination will be very short, and we hope to have another witness today. Can we start?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under Item 2 of your task, you were talking about the identity of a language and of the terminology used in the original version of all the documents. When you explained the language which was used in the documents that you studied, you concluded that the language used was the Serbian language mostly used in Western Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that it is actually the Serbo-Croatian or the Croato-Serbian that was used in Western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then also conclude that the documents which were drafted could have been drafted by either a Serb or a Croat or a Muslim, i.e., that you cannot determine the ethnic background of the person who composed, who drafted, the documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: That is largely correct. There are some features which might occur in a document which would tend to suggest that the person was of one or another ethnicity, but nevertheless, I concur.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To provide us with a more general picture, when describing the documents of the war presidency in your general conclusions, you stated that, and I quote: "In all the documents, it is the western variant of the Serbian language typical of the documents which were drafted in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the year 1992." Can we then conclude that the language in question, or its dialect, is the dialect that is used in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: We are dealing in the year 1992 with the period in which there was a tendency for members of differing ethnic or national groups to begin to differentiate their linguistic usage. That being said, it would be characteristic of the period up until this time for documents written in standard Serbo-Croatian, Croato-Serbian to be produced in a language such that you really could not distinguish the ethnicity of the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you able to establish who exactly was it who drafted the documents that you have studied, i.e., were you able to establish who was the author of these documents; and secondly, which organ was in charge of drafting these documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: This answer would vary, depending on the group of documents with which we are dealing. In the case of the draft documents of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, it was my conclusion that in a majority of instances, these documents, or perhaps in some cases, an earlier version of them not available to me, was drafted by one of the municipal administrative organs of the Prijedor municipality. In these cases, of course, I could not determine the particular individual or the exact number of individuals involved in the drafting of these documents. In general, it is a conclusion over the body of documents in this corpus that they indicated drafting for each group of documents by more than one individual, for eventual signing by the individual whose name was typed at the bottom of the document when this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With regard to this, I would like to ask you the following: Did you have an opportunity to read the finding authored by Mr. ten Camp who was the expert witness on the handwritten documents in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I am aware of the report and of the testimony. I have not read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that during Mr. Camp's testimony, an issue was raised as to the credibility of the six documents obtained from the agency for information and documentation of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina also known as AID?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you able to establish where the documents were printed? When I say that, I mean the Official Gazettes of the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: To be clear, then, let me repeat: When you're referring to documents being printed, you're referring to their publication in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: In those cases where I found in the Official Gazette an act -- publication of an act identical or almost identical in title and content with one of the documents of our corpus of documents, then I conclude that, yes, that document or that -- the act represented by that document had been published.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you cannot tell us for a fact where they were published?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: By -- in this case, by referring to where they were published, are we referring to the location where the Official Gazette was actually compiled, or where it was actually printed? Perhaps if you could be more precise in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please reply to both of these questions.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: In regard to the location where the Official Gazette was printed and where it was compiled, I recall seeing publication information indicated, either at the beginning or -- I don't recall, at the end of individual issues of the Official Gazette, which I take to be indicative of the location of printing. As for compilation, I could only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you something with regard to letter K. Are you aware of the fact that in entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless of the script, whether it is Cyrillic or Latinic, K is used in its Latinic version, unlike in Serbia when Cyrillic is used there, then the Cyrillic version of a letter K, a short K, is used?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: As I said before, I've less experience in the Cyrillic handwritings of Bosnia than in Serbia, and I believe that the extended K that I have seen, or K, that I have seen in these documents is -- main not be anything more than a personal idiosyncracy. In terms of can I generalise between the difference of Cyrillic used in Serbia and that used in Bosnia, I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I am emphasising. This is not a personal idiosyncracy; it is a general feature present all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. So you are not familiar with the fact that this is a general thing, a general feature all over Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with such a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the photocopied signatures before the war and after the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina must not be authenticised by a stamp. The only thing that is allowed is on the opposite side, to use a special stamp by which it is certified that the signature on the front page is original.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I am, first of all, not an attorney. Second of all, I cannot claim to have full knowledge of the laws and regulations which governed the preparation of documents in the Former Yugoslavia and its republics. I have some familiarity with some such regulations which I have gained through my employment and research here. But I cannot claim expertise in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Having lived in Serbia for five years, were you ever in a position to receive a document with a photocopied signature authenticised by the original stamp? That document may have been either for your personal use or for your official use. Has it ever happened?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I do not recall. It may or may not have. But I do not recall whether it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I put it to you that this should not have taken place?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I cannot answer to you whether it should or should not have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Talking about stamps and seals, having looked at the documents that you studied for your report, have you ever noticed an irregular use of a stamp or seal?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Sir, I don't understand what you mean by an "irregular use" of a stamp or a seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that you came across a situation in which a stamp belonging to one body or organ was used to certify or authenticise a document produced by another body or organ?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't give you as precise an answer as you might desire and should receive. It's not a question that I have thought out. I have at various times in my work seen documents that were produced, or at least purportedly produced, by some body at the beginning of its existence, or near to the beginning of its existence, and which may have had a stamp that you would not have expected it to have. But I'm sorry, I cannot give you a more precise answer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to remind you about documents produced by the Serbian Democratic Party, documents marked by the letter A, so the first group of documents. When you are talking about the seal, you said that two seals or stamps were used. The first one was the stamp of the BH SDS of the municipal board of Prijedor; and the second stamp was the stamp of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian Assembly of the Prijedor Municipality. Did it ever happen to you that the documents produced by one body were certified by different seals or stamps?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: This is in my recollection the only time that I have encountered a document with two distinct stamps on it. Again, it may well be the case that I'm forgetting some previous example, but I recall none.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also mention in your report the seals with a number 4 and a number 8, and perhaps with number 3. Can you, please, explain the nature of these seals.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: These are stamps, and I will distinguish between a stamp and a seal. What we -- to what we find on our documents, I refer to this as a stamp. These are documents -- I'm sorry. These are stamps which read Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Prijedor Municipality, Municipal Assembly Prijedor, if I remember correctly. But approximately this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you find them on the documents produced by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor or also on the documents produced by some other bodies? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I found these stamps primarily on documents of the Crisis Staff, and in one instance, on a document of the Municipal Assembly. I'm sorry, perhaps I can also note that we have very few documents of the Municipal Assembly in this corpus that are not drafts in any case. There are very few stamps at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the meaning of these numbers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I am only familiar with having seen them and having had the opportunity to attempt to infer their meaning. But other than that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we have touched upon the documents produced by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, you stated that you analysed 28 documents all together. Having looked at your report, I found that you had established that none of these documents had been signed. Do you remember, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I recall that one bears a stamp, but I would have to refer to my notes to recall whether I state that actually none is signed. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, you say in your report that you came across one with a signature. Can we then conclude - and this can be seen in your report - that the rest of them, that is, the remaining 27, do not have a signature?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: That would be the natural inference. But again, I would want to simply refer back to the report itself to see what I have said there. Otherwise, what I have said there stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If this is what your report says, will you then adhere to what is written in it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, the majority of these documents do not bear a file number. This is what is says in your report, the only exception being the first document, 172. For all the others, you say that they do not bear a date. They -- but they do bear some sort of a number in the form of a number, but no number is complete.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: It is my recollection that certainly the large majority of these documents are not signed. They have either no reference number or they have what appears to be a partial reference number or perhaps better referred to as the form for a reference number to be filled in at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we may conclude that these documents are draft documents, not final documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: That was my conclusion, certainly in the majority of these instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this group of documents, when providing your comments on the Document Number S110, this is a decision by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor published in the Official Gazette unsigned without a seal, typed, as signed by Dr. Milorad Stakic [as interpreted] himself. And there are a number of such documents, similar documents in a sequence. In brakets you conclude the following: This shows that he himself personally signed this document, or that maybe somebody else provided a place or envisaged that he would be the one who would eventually sign this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop for a moment because the transcript if frozen. I think it will happen as it was yesterday that it will reappear within a few minutes as such. So if the parties want, we can proceed. If one or the other regards this as an obstacle, we should stop because I think new text will get lost. Let me take the opportunity, it is correct what we can read on the transcript, Dr. Milorad Stakic himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I think that I said Milomir Stakic. But -- or maybe I made a mistake. I try to [inaudible] somebody else. But I'll restate my questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question, sir. Does this demonstrate that Dr. Milomir Stakic had already signed this document, or that somebody a third person had decided that eventually he would sign the document which was at that time just a draft?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: May I ask for a clarification. Is this question in regard to the published form of the acts that we see in the Official Gazette with the SR next to it, and are you asking for my interpretation of the meaning of that SR?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about documents which were published in the Official Gazette, and since there are obviously no signatures in the Official Gazette. And we could see that the signature of Dr. Milomir Stakic appeared in several versions, and this is one of the problems in this case. My question to you is as follows: Can you claim with certainty if one reads this SR in the Official Gazette, then can one be sure that Dr. Milomir Stakic indeed signed this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I should perhaps best answer this question with an "on the one hand" and "the other hand." On the one hand, I cannot state with certainty that such documents were indeed signed by Dr. Milomir Stakic, as I do not see the signature. On the other hand, I, as a reader, seeing this SR interpret it as an assertion that the document from which the Official Gazette was compiled contained a signature of Dr. Milomir Stakic. And I would also note in this regard that I have seen in the Official Gazette one or more acts of the Crisis Staff below which appears not Dr. Milomir Stakic by his own hand or personally, but rather, if I recall directly, Dr. Milan Kovacevic presiding over the Crisis Staff by his own hand rather than Dr. Milomir Stakic president of the Crisis Staff by his own hand. This, I take to be an indication that when the document from which the Official Gazette was compiled did not contain a signature of or perhaps even for Dr. Milomir Stakic, but bearing the name of some other individual, then that could be reflected in the wording of the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this was reflected in the Official Gazette at all times?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Such certainty I cannot provide, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report, sir, you state that the documents which were already divided into categories, that is to say, the document emanating from the municipal assembly, the document from the Crisis Staff, war presidency, and national defence documents, that such documents are written on different typewriters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Perhaps I should make one clarification in the course of answering the question. Your question asks whether these documents which were already divided into categories, and then the question continues. The division into categories was done by myself initially as a tool simply to make my task a little bit easier in the expectation that this might turn out to be a significant categorisation. Now, as for the question itself, again, two parts. First of all, I am not an expert on the identification or distinction between typewriters. That being said, certain gross characteristics occasionally allow one to state clearly that two documents were not printed on the same typewriter. And yes, various typewriters were used in the production of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were drafting your report, you were also able to recognise or realise that there was some discrepancies in determining the numbering of the documents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I believe that your question refers to the reference numbers, the 01- et cetera or 023 or similar?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I did note some other discrepancies or one might better say anomalies, unexpected facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you've also talked about the water stamp on the paper itself. You've also stated that a few documents had a very similar water stamp. But you've also said that a -- various numbers of papers were used. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that refer to each category? In other words, when we talk about the documents, for instance, of the Municipal Assembly, were they using various types of paper?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I should perhaps refer to my notes before answering the question. However, I'm quite certain the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In a general way, could we say that for all the other categories of documents, the same situation prevails? If I helped you, would you be able to point out to me the various qualities of papers in different categories?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I believe that the same conclusion will hold for the various categories. In some cases, the difference in paper type is manifest. In some cases, differences may be due to aging of the paper and I would not be qualified necessarily to distinguish between the paper types. But I think that what you're stating is probably correct. I would -- I think it is probably correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Doctor. No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only one additional question emanating from this huge table, and please extend also to your staff members our gratitude for preparing this document. It facilitates and it brings some order. One question: When you made the categorisation, did you ever find a reason why some documents were signed by the last name or others with this S. Milomir, emphasising this -- the first name or the given name?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I can attempt to infer and answer from the documents themselves. I would note first that the form of the signature is correlated with the script. The S. Milomir signature is the Latin, in the Latin script. The Stakic or M. Stakic signature is in the Cyrillic script. I further infer that, and under the assumption, under the assumption that these signatures are authentic, I realise I am not competent to make that determination. But if we assume this, then I can state that the predominant signature is the one in Latin script of S. Milomir. We see this script in the very earliest document, I believe, of the corpus from I believe it is November of 1991. We see it in a variety of documents from 1992. And we see it again in a document from 1996. The Cyrillic signature is certainly used less. It may be overgeneralising from the -- it is overgeneralising perhaps from the amount of evidence available to me bestowed that the Cyrillic signature was used for perhaps only a short period of time, but this is the inference that I would be tempted to reach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From your experience working with other material, can you state whether or not there was a certain period of time it became, let's say, it became modern or to use preferably to just sign with the given name instead of the entire name, as we know it? For example, from earlier periods in time in communist systems that it was the habit to use, first of all, the first name?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW CORIN
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question affirmatively. I'm aware of no such popularity of the use of first names in signing documents. At the same time, I would, not from my experience in dealing with documents from Bosnia-Herzegovina, but -- or from the former Yugoslavia, but simply from more general experience suggest that perhaps people will sign their names in a less formal manner, sometimes in a more formal manner at different times. But that's the extent of the answer that I can provide for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions? Judge Fassi Fihri? No. Judge Vassylenko? I can see no further questions. Thank you very much for your efforts. You're excused. And may madam usher please escort the witness out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to announce that it will not be possible to proceed with another witness due to the fact that we would need a change in the booth because we have different languages. In this case, as you know, Mr. Sebire will prepare in French. And therefore, the video, would this be ready and which period of time would it take?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The video is available, and I think it's about 10 or 15 minutes long. I don't think any longer than that. However, Mr. Sebire, although not entirely pleased, would be able and willing to listen to the question in French and testify in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think, to be more accurate, it's better to proceed with the video. And we have at least two issues we have to discuss in the presence of three Judges. There is the Prosecutor's seventh notice for admission of transcript pursuant to Rule 92 bis, and the Prosecutor's eighth notice. We discussed the seventh in brief in a Status Conference, but no doubt it has to be repeated in open court. At that time, in the Status Conference, parties were asked to come to an agreement on the admission of this transcript. Did you succeed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't recall discussing it. But if I could briefly summarise, I think there was some confusion, at least on my part, originally about this witness. This was a witness who testified on Keraterm, and the witness does describe several things but the most important is hearsay regarding he met a man in the woods who was a survivor of the massacre - he reported - the massacre of people taken from Keraterm on the 5th of August, the day the camp closed. These were the people, testimony has come out at this trial, about a a hundred or so names, 120 names or so were called out. They were loaded on to two buses. There was testimony from Witness B that the intervention squad was there, and Darko Mrdja was there. That those buses - there was other evidence from Witness A and others - that those busses arrived at Omarska camp and a few additional prisoners were placed on the buses. Some of those individuals have been exhumed and identified from Hrastova Glavica exhumation site that Mr. Sebire talked about. This witness speaks about the man in the woods telling about him that massacre and, in fact, describing how people were lined up at the pit at Hrastova Glavica, though he did use another word for that site which he uses in his testimony, which is Lusci Palanka. So we think it's important evidence. He also describes an attack upon his village, which I don't recall the name of right now, beginning with a Z, that we didn't have evidence of, his first-hand experience on that attack. And just to further inform the Court, the individual who reported this to the witness in the woods subsequently disappeared. So he cannot testify. Presumed dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear observations by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think at this late stage that it would be highly prejudicial to allow any more evidence or testimony in connection with any of the factors since we have one remaining very limited witness who has already been cross-examined. Our second objection to this is that it would deprive Dr. Stakic his fundamental right to cross-examine a witness on critical issues, both as to the date and time.
