Third, if I understood -- of death and the crimes that are underlying this particular indictment. Third, if I understand Mr. Koumjian, this might be actually considered also cumulative evidence which would be prohibited so far as he has brought and led evidence which has established in part, although now I understand that they are trying to clarify that issue. But nonetheless, the evidence is in. They are about to close their case. For those three reasons, we would ask the Court reject their motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could just clarify, this witness, I think we applied for this witness quite some time ago but were waiting the lifting of protective measures which just arrived in the -- a few days before we filed the motion, the President lifted the protective measures. The witness does not speak about Dr. Stakic. It is all crime-based. It is not cumulative, in my view, because it is unique evidence regarding what happened to those buses and also what happened in his village which there is no other evidence regarding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I understand that the original witness is, yes, to put it this way, not available for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The witness who testified in the Keraterm case reported the man in the woods telling him about this, and that person is missing and presumed dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, before deciding on this issue, let's turn to the eighth Prosecution notice. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me correctly in connection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. We do object to that. Specifically, we object to it because we did not have an opportunity to cross-examine Bernard O'Donnell in connection with the testimony that he offered in another case regarding -- specifically, the facts underlying the issues in which he testified in this case are far different from those that he has offered in the other case. We believe that we should not respectfully try a case in a vacuum and bring in testimony of individuals, such as Mr. O'Donnell, in other cases, and then having given the Defence an opportunity to cross-examine him on a limited basis, namely, the arrest of Dr. Stakic last year and the issues relating to the chain of custody of documents that were seized. The Prosecution should have at that time, knowing that he had some critical testimony in connection with the Variant A and B documents, should have offered that. Instead, they chose to offer a witness, Mr. Inayat, to testify in connection with the sourcing of that documentation. We strongly that we have been denied our right to cross-examine Mr. O'Donnell on that issue, and we would ask that that testimony be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a completely different subject matter than what Mr. O'Donnell testified to previously. The Defence, during its examination of Mr. Inayat, raised issues about the Variant A and B document and their objection to it. And I think we indicated at the time that there was extensive evidence presented in the Bosanski Samac case regarding various copies of that document in the possession of the OTP. That is the testimony of Mr. O'Donnell. Frankly, we do not have any objection to the Defence cross-examining Mr. O'Donnell. We presented his testimony because we think it's relevant, no need to repeat what's -- he has already stated on direct and at least two cross-examinations in that case, extensive testimony in that case regarding the various sources of the Variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell would be available tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would have to check. We can quickly check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can do it whilst we are having a look on the video. One final question in the direction of the Defence: Today you provided, I think it was J17, the Prosecutor's letter presenting a huge number of documents under Rule 68. Is there --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, D29 for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, indeed. It's late not only in the day, but also in the case. You know the letter from the Prosecution presenting these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have the concrete question: Do you think, and if yes, why, that you are limited in the exercise of your rights in the framework of a fair trial by this late presentation of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. I do have extensive comments that I was going to share with the Court in our Status Conference in connection with what I believe are the violation of both the spirit and letter of Rule 68. In connection with the witness that was before us these last couple days, Mr. Brown, I do not believe that the documents given to us at this late stage, namely, the day of his initial direct testimony, prejudices the Defence so long as not only the letter offered by the OTP in connection with these 97 items that are listed under Rule 68 is admitted into evidence, but we would also move that in their entirety, those 97 documents be admitted so that the Defence can in an attempt to provide the Court an objective argument in connection with the documents from either the police or the MUP, SUP, and the political civilian authorities. I would like to have the opportunity reserve my remarks in detail in connection with what I believe was a, and indeed continues to be, a violation of Rule 68. But specifically in connection with this letter and the Exhibit D29, the Defence believes that so long as the documents are introduced and admitted into evidence as offered by the Prosecution to us, we would not be claiming that we were prejudiced vis-a-vis the witness that testified relating to these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, if provided with these documents and they are admitted into evidence, then you would not request a continuation of the Prosecutor's case and not a continuation or reopening of the cross-examination of Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To be perfectly frank, Your Honour, we believe that the Defence witnesses, should we come to the Defence case, will integrate these documents as well, although we would prefer, since the documents have been presented and produced, that they merely be admitted. And we would not be seeking for an extension of the Prosecutor's case, nor would we be seeking leave of Court to perform additional cross-examination on the witness Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I understand it that you waive your right to request to proceed with the Prosecutor's case on Monday. This would be the alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not understanding the Court. I believe that the Prosecutor's case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's very simple, a clear yes or no question. There is a possibility, if you believe there is an infringement of your rights, and you should first read and review these documents, and if based on this, have some additional questions to Witness Brown, then it would be, from our point of view, mandatory to proceed with the Prosecutor's case on Monday. So the alternative would be you are satisfied with the admission into evidence of these documents, and then come back to these documents later and leave it to you to give your submissions on the basis of these documents, and then for the Judges to evaluate this, but not necessarily discussing these documents once again with Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would take that latter option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Then I believe the time is ripe for starting the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have the transcript to distribute. The booths already have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "J: I've just one question: We are here very shortly after the parliament in Pale has discussed the Geneva plan. How do you feel personally about this Geneva plan? "MS: That it was accepted? To start from the other end, I think that at this moment, the Serbian assembly, in fact, the members of the Republika Srpska People's Assembly, that they have now realised the whole weight of the pressure and threats concerning a possible air intervention. And with some corrections that were originally offered, that plan, in fact, the solution, a constitutional solution for a future system of new Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they after all, to my opinion, did a good thing by accepting this plan. In this way, they showed that they are in favour of a peaceful resolution of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they are against the war, regardless of the shortcomings of this constitutional solution, which is to the disadvantage of the Serbian people. "And for the very Geneva solution, if we have the constitutional solution in mind, provinces are possible here; however, it should be allowed to have provinces of the three constitutional peoples, that Serbian provinces may be allowed to join and live and exist as a distinctive institution in the future Bosnia and Herzegovina. Secondly, that the constitution is adopted by a consensus and also changed by those means and not to have a unitary Muslim state. "As far as the maps are concerned, I think that they've been created based on the propaganda by Alija Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman, and the Vatican and Tehran, and they are not [as interpreted] a result of the real, factual state of affairs on the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. So that the territory of Kozara and Grmac was never Turkish; and according to the plan offered in Geneva, it has now been given to some kind of Cazin region, which is almost completely Serbian, over 70 per cent Serbian. "J: Over 110 Muslim towns crossed over to the Croat side... Do you think that there is a possibility of direct negotiations with the Muslim side regarding that? "MS: First of all, it is essential that this should be agreed in Geneva. It's a big step forward that they came to holding bilateral talks, talks between the warring sides. Secondly, to end the war. And thirdly, that the European monitors should come to the field to determine the factual state of affairs so that they don't make maps, projections, and constitutions based on the propaganda from Vatican and Tehran. One has to come to Prijedor to see who lives here, who works, what they work, what they activities are going on there. Go to Krupa or to Novi, to Sanski Most - I'm talking about cities that are of interest here - to determine, to see for themselves what the situation really is, who lives there and what they are doing. Then they should go away, take a week and or so, and draw new maps. "J: ...To build the city again, though there are plans... "MS: Before that, I would go back to the previous question about what happened to the Muslim population of Kozarac and Prijedor. In February and March of last year, that is, 1992, an organised exodus of Muslim women and children had began from the territory of the Prijedor municipality, which is one of the proofs that they were preparing for a war, apart from other proofs such as arming themselves, stock-piling food in dugouts, and so on. "Secondly, we have information that over 50 buses were organised and left via Zagreb and Ljubljana towards Europe. Also, hundreds and hundreds of people left by their own arrangement. During the war, many have fled over Kozara, running away from the collection centres. These were not concentration camps. There were no fortifications, no barbed wire, electricity, nor mine fields, and they were guarded by twentish guards. And in the true sense of the word, we do not have information on the number of killed and missing. However, the number of 5.000, that -- when one hears it, one should get hold of one's chair. That number is not even one tenth of what you've presented. "As far as Kozarac now is concerned, the sawmill was opened and started working again. It would work to a fuller capacity, but it does not due to the lack of electricity. A few shops and cafes have been opened. The health-centre is open. And of course, they have as much electricity as any other citizen of the Prijedor municipality. This has already been installed: Electricity, water, supply and sewage system. A plan has been drawn up to repair houses that are completely damaged and not inhabitable, and the other ones that have been marked, the ones that are inhabited, they are generally being inhabited. And the other ones that are for repair are to be repaired. "The people who live there are Serbs who had already lived there; Ukrainians, Croats, Serb refugees from Central Bosnia, i.e., from the parts of Bosnia where power is held by Croats and Muslims. From the time being in Kozarac, Muslims are in the smallest number because they either do not wish to come back or are afraid, or they are waiting for the outcome of this war. So maybe even those who did not stain their hands with Serbian blood will possibly come back." "J: A woman told us that she fled from Kladusa and that what she wants now is to go back to her house and she doesn't want to live in a Muslim house. Is it realistic to expect after all these conflicts that the refugees who fled their homes will return, all of them, including the Muslims?" "MS: It depends on the future organisation on Bosnia-Herzegovina, on how the state will be arranged. There, what is being considered is a form of a confederation, or three separate states. If it is arranged so that each constitutive nation, within its unit - Republika Srpska or Herzeg-Bosnia or Central Bosnia, which would be Muslim - has the right to draft its own constitution, to create its own system, to have its own police and so on and so forth, and it should guarantee, like Republika Srpska and its constitution guarantee, full democracy and the rights to other peoples and ethnicities which live on its territory. That's Article 10 of the Constitution. Then one should expect from the Croat side as well to guarantee to the Serb minority the right to live normally on its territory, to live equally, and at the same level of human dignity. Also, the Muslim side. "If things are organised in such a way, then one can expect that some of these families will return to their homes. I don't have any reason to doubt your statement; I was told the same. However, I must admit that these cases are few and far between. You should ask those from Bugojno, Livno, Zenica, from other municipalities controlled by Croats and Muslims, whether they want to return at all. Those who have fled with just a bundle. These people were lucky, the ones that are close to Glina municipality which belongs to the Republika Srpska Krajina. They are in the vicinity of UNPROFOR, so they got out on that side, and then via Dvor and Novi came here. "J: So these people, the Muslims who are now refugees, and they live in refugee camps in Germany. If they so wanted, will they be allowed to return? "MS: This is what I was just about to add. In all of this, in this war, regardless of the fact that it's not yet finished and one doesn't know when it will finish, jihad gained the most. Because the aim of forming a Muslim state in Europe -- and the Balkans, whether Europe wants to admit it or not, is a part of Europe geographically. Jihad has won because a great number of Muslims from this region have emigrated and have gone to Germany, i.e., across Europe. "Why am I mentioning this? Because all of these Muslims from this region had a choice, whether to go to Zenica, Sarajevo, Travnik or Western Europe. They have chosen Western Europe. They wouldn't even hear of Zenica. They didn't even want to go to Croatia. They know that they are not welcome there. They go to Europe for economic reasons, and the reasons preached to them by jihad. "But let's go back to your question. Regardless of the final outcome of all of this, here in Prijedor, as the chief of SUP told you, things have been processed so neatly that some countries would be envious, even in peacetime. Such a great number of people have been processed. Some fifty experts, crime inspectors, have worked here to determine what the state of affairs is. They have worked around the clock. We have so much material that those who have stained their hands with blood will not be able to return. The others, if they want, they will be able to return. "MK: A large percentage of Muslims have not been expelled from here. Those who have not bloodied their hands, who haven't sinned. There is a rule that dictates migrations of population in the world. This is probably something primordial in humans who move wherever the situation is better. Western Europe had a filter through which it let in those it needed. "UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: [Indiscernible] " MK: Many, and not only Muslims, but also Croats and Serbs, have used the opportunity and have gone to seek a better life, and they have gone to Western Europe. Europe has mostly accepted Muslims, but there are also Serbs and Croats who have used the circumstances and gone there. They work there for two or three or more thousands of German marks, and I work here for 70, 80 marks. I would gladly go back to Europe and work for 12.000 marks, like I did ten years ago, rather than work here for 70 marks. I mean, this is not only how Europe, Alija, and Tudjman interpret it, after all Mico, too, that these are only war activities and cleansing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just -- I believe that the heading of the draft translation may be misleading regarding the date of the interview. The date of the interview was apparently the 22nd of January, 1993. It may have been broadcast in 1994, but it was 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any mandatory contributions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if they are mandatory, but I just have two quick observations in connection with the video that we just saw. One particularly, Your Honour, on page 98 of the transcript in between lines 8 and 9, there was another speaker that was identified. The transcript seems to not differentiate from one speaker and another. Also, within that approximately whatever the page before that, there was clearly a different person speaking, and there was also a colloquy between, at least what I have heard, the reporter and seemingly the interpreter that was not translated. I'm not sure if it is significant, but at the very least we believe that it is significant that the speakers be identified and not both be identified as "The Speaker." There may be some confusion on that at a later occasion. Also, we believe -- although Dr. Corin was here, and he would have been of great assistance to us in terms of understanding some of the words, there is in particular what we believe an inaccuracy, with due respect to the translators, specifically on line 20 of the transcript, first page, line 20. Thank you. The word he used is interpreted as "distinctive" as opposed to "unified". We would welcome the OTP to verify that and are not looking for a stipulation at this time, but are, as Dr. Corin is confident that once they check, they will probably be able to stipulate with us on that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these comments. I think we can identify at least by the initials MS and MK that -- of the transcript that there were two different persons well known to all of us. What about the admission into evidence? Was it already admitted, may I ask? May I then have, please, the next available number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I see no objections --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We would just like to share with the Court that there are Kozarski Vjesnik articles which deal with specifically this time period. We don't have an objection to the video being introduced, but we would like the opportunity to share with the Court when the time is ripe the articles that appear contemporaneously with this article that have just been provided to us - and we are grateful for it - by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then unfortunately, the transcript remains silent. What was the number once more, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: S365 for the video, and S365-1 for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And that we don't miss anything, it's the last day to the Prosecutor's case tomorrow, please recall it was on the last agenda that the Status Conference, all these documents, if possible should be available tomorrow, that we can discuss, admit or not admit them. And finally, the major issue no doubt is that it would be necessary to have available the documents included in the letter mentioned by the Defence also tomorrow, that we can go through this procedure by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I do have to announce that Mr. O'Donnell is not available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to take this into account. But even if it's a long technical exercise, these 97 documents should be here tomorrow that we can follow the plan as envisaged and agreed with by the Defence in order that we really can conclude the Prosecutor's case tomorrow. Any other remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This not being the case, this concludes today's hearing, and thank you. And apologies once again to all participants for the overtime, but when we can reach the gold, finalise the Prosecutor's case tomorrow, it will be of assistance to all of us. Trial stands adjourned until tomorrow, 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 4.22 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 27th day of September, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
